rows.stem:
(a) Define Collision frequency.
(b) Write the units of
(i) first order reaction and (ii) zero order reaction
rows.solution:
(a) Collision frequency is the number of collisions per second per unit volume of the reaction mixture. It is usually written \(Z\), and for a bimolecular gas reaction at ordinary temperature and pressure it is of the order of \(10^{25}\) collisions per litre per second — enormously more than the number of reactions that actually occur, which is why collision theory also needs an energy condition and an orientation factor.

(b) The units follow from the rate law, since the rate itself always carries units of mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\).
(i) For a first order reaction rate \(= k[\mathrm{A}]\), so \(k\) = rate divided by concentration: \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\).
(ii) For a zero order reaction rate \(= k\), so \(k\) carries the units of rate itself: mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\).

The question asks for "the units of a first order reaction" without saying whether it means the reaction's RATE or its rate CONSTANT, and the marking scheme accordingly accepts mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\) as well for part (i). Under that reading the answer is the same for every order, since a rate is a rate; it is the rate CONSTANT whose units change with the order, which is what makes the question worth asking.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(a) Why is third ionization enthalpy of manganese very high ?
(b) Why Zn, Cd and Hg are not regarded as transition elements ?
rows.solution:
(a) The third ionisation enthalpy is the energy needed to remove an electron from the \(\mathrm{M^{2+}}\) ion, and for manganese that ion is \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} = [\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^0\). A half-filled \(3d^5\) subshell is a particularly stable arrangement, with every d orbital singly occupied and all the spins parallel. Breaking into it to remove a sixth electron costs a great deal, so the third ionisation enthalpy of manganese is unusually high.

(b) A transition element is defined as one having a partially filled d subshell in its ground state or in one of its common oxidation states. Zinc, cadmium and mercury are \((n-1)d^{10}ns^2\) in the ground state, and their common ions \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{Cd^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Hg^{2+}}\) are all \((n-1)d^{10}\). The d subshell is completely filled throughout, so none of them meets the definition. It is also why they lack the properties the definition tracks — they form colourless compounds, show no variable valency to speak of, and are poor catalysts.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem:
(a) Define didendate ligand. Give an example.
(b) Indicate the type of isomerism exhibited by the given complex :
\(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)(H_2O)Cl_2]}\)
rows.solution:
(a) A bidentate ligand is one that binds to the metal through TWO donor atoms at once, so that a single ligand occupies two coordination positions and closes a ring with the metal. The oxalate ion, \(\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}}\), is an example, binding through two of its oxygen atoms; ethane-1,2-diamine is another, binding through its two nitrogen atoms.

(b) \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)(H_2O)Cl_2]}\) exhibits geometrical isomerism, that is cis-trans isomerism. The complex is square planar, so the two chlorido ligands may lie next to each other or opposite each other, giving two distinct compounds.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem:
A solution containing 8.0 g of a non-volatile solute in 100 g of diethyl ether boils at 36.86 °C whereas pure diethyl ether boils at 35.60 °C. Determine the molar mass of the solute.
(\(\mathrm{K_b}\) for diethyl ether = 2.02 K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
rows.solution:
The elevation of boiling point is
\(\Delta T_b = T_b - T_b^{\circ} = 36.86 - 35.60 = 1.26\ \mathrm{K}\)

For a non-volatile solute,
\(\Delta T_b = K_b \times \dfrac{W_B}{M_B} \times \dfrac{1000}{W_A}\)

Rearranging for the molar mass and substituting \(K_b = 2.02\) K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\), \(W_B = 8.0\) g and \(W_A = 100\) g,
\(M_B = K_b \times \dfrac{W_B}{\Delta T_b} \times \dfrac{1000}{W_A} = 2.02 \times \dfrac{8}{1.26} \times \dfrac{1000}{100}\)
\(M_B = \dfrac{16160}{126} = 128.25\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

Note that a difference of two Celsius readings is the same number as a difference of two kelvin readings, so no temperature conversion is needed here.

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem:
(a) Complete and balance the following equations :
(i) \(4\mathrm{FeCr_2O_4} + 8\mathrm{Na_2CO_3} + 7\mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow\)
(ii) \(5\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} + \mathrm{MnO_4^{-}} + 8\mathrm{H^{+}} \longrightarrow\)
(b) Explain why actinoid contraction is greater from element to element than lanthanoid contraction.
rows.solution:
(a)(i) This is the first step in extracting chromium compounds from chromite ore: the ore is roasted with sodium carbonate in air, and the chromium is oxidised from \(+3\) to \(+6\) as the yellow chromate.
\(4\mathrm{FeCr_2O_4} + 8\mathrm{Na_2CO_3} + 7\mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow 8\mathrm{Na_2CrO_4} + 2\mathrm{Fe_2O_3} + 8\mathrm{CO_2}\)

(ii) Permanganate oxidises iron(II) to iron(III) in acid solution and is itself reduced to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\):
\(5\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} + \mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 8\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 4\mathrm{H_2O} + 5\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\)

(b) Contraction across a series happens because the electrons being added shield the outer shells from the nucleus poorly, so the effective nuclear charge felt outside grows and pulls those shells in. The 5f orbitals of the actinoids are more diffuse and shield even less effectively than the 4f orbitals of the lanthanoids, so the effective nuclear charge rises faster from one actinoid to the next. The contraction per element is therefore greater in the actinoids.

rows.stem:
(a) \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{2+}}\) is paramagnetic whereas \(\mathrm{[Fe(CO)_5]}\) is diamagnetic. Justify the statement. [Atomic number of Fe = 26]
(b) On the basis of crystal field theory write the electronic configuration for \(\mathrm{d^4}\) ion if \(\Delta_0 < \mathrm{P}\).
rows.solution:
(a) Iron is \(+2\) in the first complex, so \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is \(3d^6\); in the carbonyl the metal is in the zero oxidation state, \(3d^6 4s^2\). What separates them is the strength of the ligand field.

In \(\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{2+}}\) water is a weak field ligand. The crystal field splitting is smaller than the energy needed to pair two electrons in one orbital, so the six d electrons spread out rather than pair, leaving four unpaired: the complex is paramagnetic.

In \(\mathrm{[Fe(CO)_5]}\) carbon monoxide is a strong field ligand. The splitting exceeds the pairing energy, so every electron is paired and none is left unpaired: the complex is diamagnetic.

(b) When \(\Delta_0 < \mathrm{P}\) the field is weak, so promoting an electron to the upper set costs less than pairing two in the lower one. A \(d^4\) ion therefore puts three electrons singly into the \(t_{2g}\) orbitals and the fourth into an \(e_g\) orbital:
\(t_{2g}^3\ e_g^1\)
This is the high spin arrangement, with four unpaired electrons.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the major product in the following reaction :
1-Ethyl-3-nitrobenzene \(+\ \mathrm{Br_2} \xrightarrow{\text{heat}}\) ?
(b) Define Chirality.
(c) Why racemisation occurs in \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — part (a)'s substrate is printed as a SKELETAL DRAWING: a plain hexagon carrying CH2CH3 at one vertex and NO2 three vertices round from it, followed by '+ Br2 --heat--> ?'. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
(a) Bromine with heat attacks the side chain rather than the ring, and within the side chain it takes the BENZYLIC hydrogen — the one on the carbon attached to the ring — because the radical formed there is stabilised by delocalisation into the ring. In 1-ethyl-3-nitrobenzene that is the \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) carbon:
\(\mathrm{3\text{-}O_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_2CH_3} + \mathrm{Br_2} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{3\text{-}O_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}CHBr{-}CH_3} + \mathrm{HBr}\)
The major product is 1-(1-bromoethyl)-3-nitrobenzene. The nitro group deactivates the ring, which makes side-chain attack the favoured route all the more.

(b) Chirality is the property of an object or molecule of being non-superimposable on its mirror image. A molecule with that property is said to be chiral; the commonest cause is a carbon atom bearing four different groups.

(c) An \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction passes through a carbocation intermediate, and that carbocation is PLANAR — the positive carbon is \(sp^2\) hybridised with its three bonds in one plane. The nucleophile can therefore approach with equal ease from either face, and the two approaches give the two opposite configurations in equal amounts. The product is a racemic mixture, which is optically inactive even though the starting material was not.

rows.stem:
(a) Define the following terms :
(i) Denaturation as related to proteins
(ii) Oligosaccharides
(b) On the basis of structure differentiate between Amylose and Amylopectin.
rows.solution:
(a)(i) Denaturation is the loss of a protein's biological activity when its native structure is destroyed. Heating, or a change in pH, or adding certain chemicals, disturbs the hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions holding the chain in shape; the globules unfold and the helix uncoils. The PRIMARY structure survives — the peptide bonds are not broken — but the secondary and tertiary structure is lost, and with it the activity. Coagulating the white of an egg is the everyday example.

(ii) Oligosaccharides are carbohydrates that give between two and ten monosaccharide units on hydrolysis. Disaccharides such as sucrose and maltose are the commonest members.

(b) Both are components of starch and both are built from \(\alpha\)-D-glucose, but they differ in shape. Amylose is an UNBRANCHED chain of a large number of \(\alpha\)-D-(+)-glucose units joined by \(\mathrm{C_1-C_4}\) glycosidic linkages, and it makes up about 15-20% of starch. Amylopectin is a BRANCHED polymer: its main chain uses the same \(\mathrm{C_1-C_4}\) linkages, but branches are thrown off through \(\mathrm{C_1-C_6}\) linkages roughly every 20 to 25 units, and it makes up the remaining 80-85%.

rows.stem:
(a) What products would be formed when a nucleotide from DNA containing thymine is hydrolysed ?
(b) How will you explain the presence of five -OH groups in glucose molecule which are attached to different carbon atoms ?
(c) Write the reaction of glucose with HCN.
rows.solution:
(a) Hydrolysis breaks a nucleotide into its three components, so a DNA nucleotide containing thymine gives the base thymine, the pentose sugar 2-deoxy-D-ribose, and phosphoric acid.

(b) Treat glucose with acetic anhydride. It gives a stable pentaacetate, a derivative carrying exactly five acetyl groups, and since acetylation occurs at hydroxyl groups there must be five of them:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{(\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O}} \mathrm{CHO(CH{-}OCOCH_3)_4CH_2{-}OCOCH_3}\)
That the five sit on five DIFFERENT carbons follows from the derivative being stable: two hydroxyl groups on the same carbon would make a gem-diol, which loses water at once.

(c) Hydrogen cyanide adds across the carbon-oxygen double bond of the aldehyde group at C-1, giving the cyanohydrin:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} + \mathrm{HCN} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH(OH)(CN)(CHOH)_4CH_2OH}\)
This is glucose cyanohydrin, and its formation is one of the reactions that establishes the presence of a carbonyl group in the open chain form.
